title.rendered: Nigerians should reject vote buying to have quality leadership – Ex-envoy, Gana

content.rendered:
Former Nigerian Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Japan, Prof. Yisa Gana, speaks with DARE AKOGUN on Nigeria’s foreign policy, the rising hostility towards Nigerians in some African countries, including South Africa and Côte d’Ivoire, and why he believes Nigerians should demand a change in leadership in 2027

Given your experience as a former ambassador, what is your assessment of Nigeria’s current foreign policy, especially amid growing reports of Nigerians facing deportation and xenophobic attacks in countries like South Africa and Côte d’Ivoire?

It is a shame, and a national embarrassment that a country as richly endowed as Nigeria has reached a stage where its citizens are desperate to leave for countries that are far less endowed in terms of natural and human resources.

When I served as Nigeria’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Japan, I represented the President and the Federal Republic of Nigeria with full diplomatic authority. I understand what diplomacy means and what a country’s image represents internationally. Today, what we are witnessing is a direct reflection of domestic failures. The issue is not simply that countries like South Africa, Morocco or even Libya are deporting Nigerians or treating them poorly. The real issue is why Nigerians are leaving their country in such large numbers in the first place.

Sixty-five years after independence, Nigerians are now migrating in search of opportunities to countries that should ordinarily be looking up to Nigeria as Africa’s biggest economy and one of its most resource-rich nations. That should concern every patriotic Nigerian.

This is not merely a foreign policy challenge; it is a governance challenge. Foreign policy is only as strong as the country it represents. If your economy is weak, your security is poor, unemployment is high and your citizens are frustrated, then naturally your image abroad will also suffer.

Government must begin by fixing Nigeria. If people have jobs, security, electricity and confidence in the economy, they will not be risking their lives across deserts and the Mediterranean Sea in search of opportunities elsewhere.

Some have argued that Nigeria should retaliate diplomatically whenever its citizens are deported or subjected to xenophobic attacks abroad. Would you support such a move?

No. I don’t believe retaliation is the solution. You cannot respond emotionally to every diplomatic issue. The primary responsibility of government is to make the country attractive enough for Nigerians to want to stay. Instead of threatening foreign governments, we should first ask ourselves why our citizens are leaving in the first place. What are they running away from? Many Nigerians abroad would actually like to return home, but they ask a simple question: “return home to do what?” If they come back, where are the jobs? Where is the security? Where is the electricity? Where are the opportunities for businesses to thrive?

Government should create policies that encourage Nigerians to remain in the country and also attract those in the diaspora back home. We have the resources to achieve this if they are properly managed. The answer is not retaliation. The answer is good governance.

 You have linked Nigeria’s foreign image to governance at home. What specific areas require urgent attention?

Everything begins with leadership. Government must first secure lives and property because security is the primary responsibility of every government. Without security, there can be no meaningful economic development.

Secondly, government must create employment opportunities. Young Nigerians are leaving because they do not see any future here. Industries are struggling, businesses are closing and investors are becoming discouraged.

Thirdly, government must provide reliable electricity. No modern economy can develop without stable power supply. You cannot industrialise a country when businesses spend enormous amounts on generators and alternative energy sources. Government should also ensure that public funds are used prudently. Nigerians want to see tangible projects that directly improve their lives.

 The International Monetary Fund recently questioned Nigeria’s budget implementation, while the Federal Government insisted the IMF did not have the correct facts. What is your view on the controversy?

My concern is not even what the IMF said. My concern is what Nigerians themselves can see. Year after year, ministries complain that only a small fraction of their capital allocations is released.

As someone who served in the legislature and understands how budgeting works, I know that the government prepares estimates of expected revenue and then appropriates expenditures based on those estimates. If the government eventually realises substantial portions of the projected revenue, Nigerians deserve to know why the projects contained in the budget are not fully executed. Where is the money? That is the question Nigerians should be asking.

If roads are not completed, hospitals are not equipped, schools are not upgraded, and infrastructure remains inadequate despite repeated budgets, then the government owes Nigerians an explanation.

The National Assembly also has a constitutional responsibility to carry out oversight. It should ask why budgets are repeatedly under-implemented despite available revenues.

Transparency and accountability are essential if Nigerians are to have confidence in public finance.

Do you believe the country’s current economic challenges are connected to poor implementation of budgets?

Certainly, budgets are supposed to translate government policies into practical development.

If ministries receive inadequate releases for capital projects, then naturally roads, hospitals, schools, water projects and other infrastructure will suffer.

The worrying question is where the money goes. If the government realises the expected revenue but projects remain abandoned, Nigerians deserve full disclosure.

Public finance should be transparent; every naira budgeted should be accounted for. That is the essence of responsible governance.

 Government has consistently argued that its reforms require time to produce results. Are you convinced?

No, what ordinary Nigerians are experiencing today is increasing hardship. People are battling rising food prices, high transportation costs, inflation, and declining purchasing power. Electricity remains unreliable, businesses continue to struggle, borrowing continues to increase.

When the government introduces reforms, citizens should gradually begin to experience improvements in their daily lives. Unfortunately, many Nigerians say their living conditions have become more difficult. Government policies must ultimately be judged by their impact on ordinary citizens.

Some years ago, the President stated that Nigerians should not re-elect him if electricity supply does not improve significantly before the end of his first term. How do you interpret that statement?

The President made that commitment himself. Therefore, Nigerians should objectively assess whether electricity has improved substantially. Power generation remains far below the country’s actual requirements. Nigeria requires tens of thousands of megawatts to support industrial growth and economic expansion, yet available supply remains significantly below that level.

If Nigerians conclude that the promise has not been fulfilled, then they have every democratic right to evaluate the administration based on its own commitments. That is how democracy works.

Beyond the economy, insecurity remains one of the country’s biggest concerns. How does this affect the country’s international image?

It affects it tremendously. Foreign investors pay close attention to security before investing. Tourists also consider security. Even Nigerians living abroad hesitate to return because of insecurity. A country battling persistent insecurity inevitably projects uncertainty internationally.

That is why addressing insecurity should remain the government’s highest priority. Until Nigerians feel safe in their homes, farms and highways, the country’s international reputation will continue to suffer.

 What message would you give Nigerians ahead of the 2027 general elections?

Nigerians have an opportunity to shape the future of this country through democratic means. They should insist on credible elections, they should reject vote buying, they should carefully evaluate candidates based on competence, integrity, experience and their plans for addressing Nigeria’s problems. This election should not be about personalities or political slogans; it should be about solutions.

Nigerians should ask every candidate practical questions. How will you improve electricity, how will you create jobs, how will you tackle insecurity, how will you reduce poverty, how will you improve education and healthcare and so on. Those are the issues that matter.

 Why did you decide to join ADC?

I have been in different political parties before. I have been in both the APC and the PDP. My decision to join the African Democratic Congress was based on the conviction that Nigeria requires a different direction. We believe leadership should be people-centred.

Government should focus on improving the welfare of citizens rather than merely winning elections. Our objective is to build institutions that work, strengthen accountability, improve governance and restore public confidence.

Ultimately, however, the decision belongs to Nigerians.

Nigeria has enormous potential. We have abundant natural resources, we have energetic young people, we have professionals who are succeeding across the world. The problem is not the absence of resources or talent; the problem is leadership and governance.

Once leadership becomes accountable, transparent and focused on the welfare of citizens, many of the country’s current challenges will begin to diminish.

I remain optimistic because I believe Nigerians are becoming more politically conscious. They now ask more questions; they demand greater accountability. If that continues, I believe Nigeria can still realise its enormous potential.

That is why I continue to say that Nigerians have a democratic opportunity in 2027 to determine the kind of country they want. The future of this nation ultimately lies in the hands of its citizens through the ballot box.
